images.caption: Figure 1:YANAMI:the first large-scale multimodal dialogue dataset and benchmark for stateful interaction.

Figure 2:Representative examples from YANAMI-400K.The four columns present evolving multimodal dialogues in four interaction scenarios: (a) multi-image fusion, (b) image editing, (c) world modeling, and (d) visual reasoning.
Across turns, subsequent responses retrieve, maintain, and update the accumulated dialogue state.
Colored text highlights six key capabilities.
Figure 3:Overview of the YANAMI data pipeline.The pipeline comprises four stages: (a) Data Preparation, (b) Data Construction, (c) Automatic Verification, and (d) Human Verification.
Figure 4:Distribution of the four interaction scenarios in the training and test sets.

Table 2:Results on YANAMI-Bench across four interaction scenarios.denotes models supporting image generation/editing only;denotes models supporting both understanding and generation.denotes concatenated image inputs;denotes placing all available images at the beginning; anddenotes interleaved image–text inputs.Red,blue, andyellowcells highlight the best results among closed-source models, open-source image-editing models, and UMMs.
Underlined results denote the second-best performance within each model group.

Figure 7:Human-verification interface for YANAMI-Bench.Annotators can browse the 100 benchmark dialogues in each interaction scenario, inspect the complete multi-turn context and visual outputs, and review or revise the corresponding atomic evaluation criteria.
The interface also records whether a sample is approved or requires image refinement, supporting the exhaustive verification and correction process used to construct the final benchmark.

Table 12:Dialogue-state understanding results for Visual Reasoning.RR, CR, CT, and CU denote Reference Resolution, Context Retrieval, Constraint Tracking, and Correction Updating, respectively.
DSU Avg. is the arithmetic mean of the four capability scores.
All results are reported on a 0–100 scale, and higher values are better.
An upward arrow indicates an improvement over BAGEL.

Table 13:Understanding and visual-realization results for Visual Reasoning.SC and VQ denote State Consistency and Visual Quality, respectively.
All component and aggregate results are reported on a 0–100 scale; VQ scores are converted from their original 0–10 scale by multiplying by 10.
Overall Avg. is computed using the weighting defined in AppendixB.3.
Image-generation-only models do not provide DSU scores; a dash denotes an unsupported or unavailable component.
Modality and input-format icons follow the conventions in Table2.
An upward arrow indicates an improvement over BAGEL.

Figure 8:Complete qualitative example for Image Editing.Across seven turns, the dialogue progressively replaces and modifies visual elements while preserving the active appearance constraints, incorporating a user correction, and retrieving earlier requirements for the final composition.
The left and right panels show the first and second halves of the same dialogue, respectively.

Figure 9:Complete qualitative example for Multi-Image Fusion.The dialogue combines information from multiple visual references while tracking the intended setting, object placement, and persistent restrictions, culminating in a jointly composed visual output.
The left and right panels show the first and second halves of the same dialogue, respectively.

Figure 10:Complete qualitative example for World Modeling.The interaction requires the model to maintain the scene layout, update an initially incorrect depth relation, and render a new viewpoint while preserving the corrected spatial state and other persistent scene properties.
The left and right panels show the first and second halves of the same dialogue, respectively.

Figure 11:Complete qualitative example for Visual Reasoning.The model follows a multi-step action plan, revises the plan after a user correction, generates intermediate visual states, and subsequently retrieves those states to describe the completed sequence.
The left and right panels show the first and second halves of the same dialogue, respectively.
